inline.s: The above is still spoken in shallow terms; there is a deeper meaning in it. The single phrase 'do not speak thus' is addressed precisely to those who propagate the Mahayana Dharma — not only to the people of that time, but also to those who would later propagate the Mahayana Dharma. Not only was Subhuti warned not to speak thus; we today likewise must not speak thus. The Buddha's true intent was to exert every effort to propagate the prajna teaching. This sutra was requested by Subhuti; in the first eight assemblies he had already spoken on the Buddha's behalf, which shows that Subhuti was a man who propagated prajna. Later the text repeatedly says that there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and explain it to others. The Buddha's hope that prajna be propagated is evident here. Had he spoken thus, would that have been the intent of propagation? And yet to propagate prajna is truly not easy. In our own country, for instance, since the Song dynasty the ancient worthies, seeing that the prajna teaching is hard to practice, were mostly unwilling to expound it. They thought that beings' karma was deep and their obstacles heavy, that they clung to marks in every way and could not easily comprehend; and they feared that people hearing this teaching would instead fall into one-sided emptiness, or even arrive at a wicked grasping at emptiness, so that it was better not to expound it at all. The World-Honored One foresaw this long ago, and therefore laid down 'do not speak thus' as a precept. That expounding prajna should instead bring on such ills as falling into one-sided emptiness is the fault of the expounder who does not propagate it well, not the fault of the hearers. One should know that prajna is precisely the Buddha-seed. This sutra says: 'All Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.' If it is not expounded, the principle of prajna can never be made clear — would that not be cutting off the Buddha-seed? Hence one cannot but exert every effort to propagate it; and this is why the later text has the words 'shoulder the Tathagata's anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.'

In recent times the great virtuous ones for the most part did not expound prajna, but expounded the perfect fusion of the three truths, which is truly not easy to understand. The Buddha spoke of the three truths at the Lotus assembly, which came right after his exposition of prajna. Therefore the Buddha forewarned him with 'do not speak thus,' requiring Subhuti to propagate this teaching. His meaning was: if you do not propagate it, how can people be brought to understand it and give rise to true faith? You worry only that beings find it hard to believe, and forget the great matter of propagating prajna — how could that be acceptable? Nor is that all: if you do not propagate it, you obstruct others' good thoughts; hence you should propagate it with all your strength. Yet if one propagates it without care, that too will not do. The Buddha expounded prajna only in his later years. When he first attained the Way he first spoke the Avatamsaka. For in this kalpa Shakyamuni is already the fourth Buddha, and since it was so long since the last Buddha, he could not but set forth the Buddha's realm completely. Yet then he turned back to expound the Agamas, to make people practice in their own persons. When people's faculties had gradually ripened, he expounded the Vaipulya, making clear the principle of the Mahayana and turning people from the small toward the great. Only after this did he expound prajna. From this one can see that this teaching requires care. Since it must both be propagated and handled with care, he had to select those whose foundation lay in keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. The Buddha's meaning was: you fear that people will not easily give rise to true faith, and worry that those who do give rise to it are few; you need only propagate as I have said and work hard in practice, and then the hearers will not be misled. It depends only on the method of the one who propagates — why worry that the hearers will not give rise to true faith? The single phrase 'do not speak thus' is of the utmost importance; those who propagate the Buddha-Dharma to the ends of the future should all be like this.

'After the Tathagata's extinction' — 'extinction' means deliverance. Deliverance has two meanings. In its fundamental sense it refers to the mind that is neither born nor extinguished. As it is said, when birth-and-death is extinguished, quiescent extinction appears before one, and this is called nirvana. Later the term was borrowed, so that whenever a Buddha or bodhisattva passes into quiescence it is also called entering extinction. 'After the extinction' means after all the Tathagata's marks of birth and death have been extinguished, which must refer to the extinction of the manifestation body. The Tathagata is the dharma-body — why then speak of extinction? There is a subtle and profound principle here. Because the Buddha wished us to understand it, he specifically said 'the Tathagata's extinction,' and this has three essential meanings:

(1) The reward body and the manifestation body are both marks; what is extinguished is the extinction of the reward and manifestation bodies. The World-Honored One's putting on his robe and eating his food, and the extinction of the ordinary-being marks that he manifested — this is the extinction of the manifestation body. The reward body too is manifested from the dharma-body; since there is manifestation, there is also extinction. That the text does not say the manifestation and reward bodies are extinguished is to show clearly that the Tathagata will never again manifest a manifestation or reward body, so that we may be alert. One should know that even the manifestation and reward bodies displayed by the Tathagata are still birth and death. As it is said, 'whatever has marks is false and delusive' — how much more so our stinking skin-bag! Moreover, as for our bodily form, we do not know why it is born, nor why it perishes; we are wholly dragged along by the power of karma and cannot be our own masters. The Buddha is not like this. Though the manifestation and reward bodies are birth and death, the Tathagata is his own master: when he wishes to be born, he is born; when he wishes to be extinguished, he is extinguished. We all possess the Tathagata-store; we should quickly return to our original face.

(2) To realize the original nature is called the Tathagata; yet the dharma-body is without marks — how can it be seen? What can be seen is a mark: what bodhisattvas see is only the reward body manifested from the dharma-body, and what ordinary beings see is the manifestation body manifested from the dharma-body. Yet if one can see that the manifestation and reward bodies are not marks, then one sees the Tathagata. Therefore, if one would see the nature, one must see it through non-mark, and must not fall into annihilation. Hence we are warned that to see the Tathagata is by no means easy, and that one must advance with courage and vigor in order to realize it. If we would see the Tathagata, we should seek him in the nature. When we speak of the nature, then I and the Tathagata, self and other, are not two; to comprehend something of one's own nature-essence is already an occasion for seeing the Tathagata.

(3) The Tathagata's reward and manifestation bodies do indeed enter extinction and are indeed marks. But they are not extinguished forever; they will still be manifested. One should know that the reward and manifestation bodies are still shadows of the dharma-body. When we know that the dharma-body is not extinguished, then the reward and manifestation bodies again have their occasions for manifestation. From ancient times there have been those who saw the sixteen-foot golden body; those who, advancing with courage and vigor, saw a Buddha-body a thousand feet tall, as the arhats did; and those who saw a great body like Mount Sumeru, which is the reward body seen by bodhisattvas. Again, when Master Zhiyi finished commenting on the Lotus Sutra, he personally saw the assembly on Vulture Peak, still seated and not yet dispersed — all these are proofs of it. Hence the first meaning: that the Tathagata will not again manifest a reward or manifestation body, so that we may be alert. The second meaning: to make people know that if they would see the Tathagata, they must work upon themselves. The third meaning: to say that the Tathagata is not extinguished, and that if only one works hard, one may still see him.

The phrase 'in the last five hundred years' has traditionally had three explanations. (1) Taking 'after' in the sense of after the Tathagata's extinction, it refers to the five hundred years following the Tathagata's extinction. (2) Taking the first five hundred years after the Tathagata's extinction as the former, the second five hundred as the middle, and the third five hundred as the latter. (3) It means the fifth five-hundred-year period after the Tathagata's extinction. For the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma each last a thousand years, and the Dharma-ending age ten thousand years, so this refers precisely to the first five hundred years of the final age. In the thousand years of the True Dharma after the Tathagata's extinction, during the first five hundred years liberation was firm; during the next five hundred, meditative concentration was firm. 'Liberation' means realizing prajna-paramita and passing beyond all suffering and distress. 'Firm' means that beings' faculties were firm. In the next five hundred years the faculties were somewhat poorer, yet people could still abide in meditative concentration. This liberation and concentration are precisely concentration and wisdom, and so it is called the True Dharma. In the first five hundred years of the thousand years of the Semblance Dharma, though there were still those who attained liberation and concentration, they were already very few; people devoted themselves to discussing principle and did not value practice, and so it is called 'firm in much hearing.' One should know that reading sutras puts the weight on contemplation; to occupy oneself merely with much hearing is like counting another's treasure, with not a penny of one's own — it is also called 'talking of food without being filled.' The World-Honored One told Ananda that many kalpas before, he had cultivated together with him, and that to this day he remained the Buddha's attendant; his failing lay precisely in attending only to much hearing. In the next five hundred years, though even those of much hearing were few, beings knew only to build temples and erect pagodas, and so it is called 'firm in pagodas and temples.' During this thousand years the forms of the Buddha-Dharma still remained, but its original intent was already lost; it was merely a semblance, and so it is called the Semblance Dharma. By the first five hundred years of the Dharma-ending age the Buddha-Dharma had declined further, and beings knew only strife — what the new vocabulary calls struggle. The early extinction of the Buddha-Dharma in India was because strife had already become widespread in the Semblance Dharma period. It was the same in our country: in the middle of the Tang dynasty, the Chan, Pure Land, and Consciousness-Only schools all raised sectarian disputes. Hence it is called 'firm in strife.' The 'last five hundred years' of this sutra refers precisely to this time. Now we are again five hundred years further on within the Dharma-ending age. Therefore the Buddha said that at such a time, if there are people who can read this sutra, they are truly rare indeed.
'Taking these as true' refers precisely to those who can keep the precepts and cultivate merit. This has four meanings.

(1) Prajna is right wisdom; wisdom is born of concentration, and concentration is born of the precepts. Therefore, if one would give rise to the right wisdom of prajna, one must work at the precepts; otherwise there is no way to give rise to concentration and wisdom. Only when an ordinary being can keep the precepts can he be free of outward defilement. If he does not keep the precepts, his mind is not pure, he cannot gather his mind to one point, he cannot contemplate, and how could he give rise to prajna? If one seeks to give rise to wisdom without keeping the precepts, one may well fall into a wicked grasping at emptiness. Therefore merit and wisdom must both be cultivated, like the two wheels of a cart, neither of which may be lacking. Only thus can the cultivator become the One Worthy of Offerings. Moreover, the two must be equal, with neither taken lightly. Some say that wisdom alone suffices; they do not realize that to stress wisdom and slight merit is to lack great compassion, and that this is utterly impermissible. Hence the Buddhas teach people to bring forth the mind of great compassion. This sutra speaks of giving at its very opening, which is enough to show that one who cultivates wisdom cannot fail to cultivate merit. If one does not cultivate merit, one has no affinity with living beings. Not only is there no affinity: even the cultivator's excellent marks cannot be complete. For those who propagate the Buddha-Dharma, excellent marks are also of importance; hence the sutras everywhere speak of the excellent marks of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. That the marks of an arhat do not equal the Buddha's has its reason. It was said above that after realizing the essence one must manifest marks — this is all for the sake of living beings, for those who see excellent marks are easily moved to draw near. The prajna teaching is what enables people to become Buddhas; keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is the foundation for becoming a Buddha.

(2) One should know that those who keep the precepts must have few desires and be content, with comparatively little greed. Only such people can practice prajna without going wrong. For the practice of prajna requires detachment from marks, and one whose greed is great can never be detached. One who cultivates merit must deeply believe in cause and effect: worldly people, wishing to obtain fame and profit, seek them according to worldly ways, while such a person seeks according to the Buddha-Dharma. Therefore one who deeply believes in cause and effect will never lean toward the mark of annihilation. To not dwell in marks, those who keep the precepts are the most suited; to not fall into the mark of annihilation, those who cultivate merit are the most suited. But when one whose greed is great hears of prajna, he falls into many faults. Some distort 'not dwelling in marks,' thinking that doing evil does not matter; they talk wildly and loftily and stop at nothing, imagining all the while that they have deeply grasped the principle of prajna; they may even kill living beings and commit sexual misconduct, and regard it all as not dwelling in marks. Therefore the Buddha does not accept such people; he must select those of few desires and contentment.

(3) The preceding text said that one who brings forth the mind to practice prajna should practice giving, and giving is relinquishment. These two kinds of people are those who can relinquish: those who keep the precepts can relinquish the desires of the world, while those who cultivate merit relinquish their own wealth and spirit, giving others wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness — and this accords precisely with the principle of prajna.

(4) In cultivating this teaching, one should first block up the gate of the mark of no-dharma. Keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is precisely blocking up the mark of no-dharma. One need only further contemplate the marks of dharmas over a long time, and if one does not grasp at the marks of dharmas, one may then succeed. Therefore the Buddha selected these two kinds of people; from this it is clear that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is nothing other than pointing directly at those who study the prajna teaching. And it is also said to us: if we would study prajna, we must do no evil and practice all good. Not doing evil is the precepts; practicing good is merit. Only by carrying these out in earnest and making the foundation firm will it do. These two kinds of people are cautious and meticulous and can let go of everything; otherwise they cannot enter prajna. That they can give rise to faith is because faith is the gate of entry to the Way. Only by practicing thus can one enter the gate; otherwise mere talk cannot enter it.

Someone says that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is the root of practicing prajna, and that one must first block up one-sided emptiness. That is so; yet there is still a doubt. The sutra plainly says 'take these as true' — but these two kinds of people are, after all, deficient in knowledge, so how can they understand the true essential meaning of this sutra? There is an important principle here. Why? Because they are blessed by the Buddha's empowerment. Such people are the faculties the Buddha has selected; if they can act according to the Buddha's words, keeping the precepts and cultivating merit, they will surely receive the Buddha's empowerment and so be able to take these as true. Students of the Buddha must, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, at every moment, seek the empowerment of the Three Jewels. Whatever practice one undertakes, it is thus. Even when expounding the sutras one must set aside one's ordinary views and seek the empowerment of the Three Jewels. To be free of this thought is to have not yet given rise to faith. Take Buddha-recitation: when reciting, one must cast aside all one's ordinary views, so that the mind holds nothing at all, and single-mindedly seek Amitabha's empowerment.

Yet someone else says: if so, one need only imitate the simple folk, so why does the Buddha also say that one must read and recite the Mahayana sutras? This has two meanings. (1) When one understands the sutras, one's practice becomes more excellent. When the principle is stored in the field of the eighth consciousness, then once it responds, the three insights and six spiritual powers can all arise at once. (2) If one can truly believe, one should learn from the firm faith of simple folk. But there is no help for it: the world has many middling people who will not consent to be counted simple, and so one must certainly make them understand the principle.

When the ancient worthies wrote books, their openings often contained words seeking the empowerment of the Three Jewels. When great bodhisattvas composed treatises, the prefaces to those treatises likewise said 'by the Buddha's awesome spiritual power.' This is true and not false; it is not dependence, nor is it superstition. Without such a thought, a self-view would remain, obstructing one's own spiritual nature, and how could a book or treatise be thorough? Therefore one must completely set aside self-view. In worldly teachings, Confucius constantly referred matters to Heaven, which also captures this meaning. Scholars after the Han did not understand it.
(Zi) Second, showing the thickness of former roots.

'Know that such a person has not planted good roots with one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas, but has already planted all good roots at the places of measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas.'

The previous section, from 'keeping the precepts and cultivating merit' down to 'take these as true,' is precisely what this section comments on. 'Such a person' refers to one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit; it says 'such a person' and not 'such people,' which shows that although keeping the precepts and cultivating merit are spoken of as two matters, they are in fact one, and neither may be lacking. From one Buddha to two Buddhas is already an extremely long time, who knows how many kalpas, let alone three, four, or five Buddhas. This shows that such a person planted good roots very long ago; and the World-Honored One says further that this is not all — he has planted all good roots at the places of thousands of ten millions of Buddhas. Moreover, above 'thousands of ten millions' the two words 'measureless' are added, so that the time is an inexpressibly, inexpressibly long one. Such a person has not cultivated only one good, but all goods; 'all goods' refers to the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices. This shows that such a person has cultivated prajna for an extremely long time. 'Planted roots' answers precisely to keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. Such a person's planted roots are already extremely deep; they are roots formed of all goods combined, and are truly what one calls rare and commendable.

The World-Honored One knows all matters of the measureless past; this statement is true and not false. From the standpoint of us ordinary beings, such a person's keeping the precepts and cultivating merit already accords with the wondrous Way. Why? Above, as soon as the World-Honored One opened his mouth to Subhuti, he said that all classes of living beings should be led into remainderless nirvana and delivered, and that though measureless, countless, boundless beings are thus delivered, in truth no being attains deliverance — this is bringing forth the great mind. First one should deliver beings, which is not to fall into emptiness; next, that in truth no being attains deliverance, which is not to dwell in marks. Then he spoke of the great practice: one should dwell nowhere; he first spoke of not dwelling in marks, then of practicing giving — for if one dwells and does not practice, that is to fall into emptiness. In these two passages the World-Honored One repeatedly warns that one must not fall into emptiness before one may bring forth the mind and cultivate. That such a person begins at once with keeping the precepts and cultivating merit — is this not a hidden accord with the World-Honored One's words about first not falling into emptiness? Again, in the introductory section, when the World-Honored One was about to expound prajna he first manifested as an ordinary being: putting on his robe and taking his bowl is keeping the precepts, and making beings give rise to a sense of shame is cultivating merit. That such a person keeps the precepts and cultivates merit — is this not likewise a hidden accord with the World-Honored One's original intent? From this one can see that unless one had planted good roots since long ago, one could not thus secretly accord with the wondrous Way. Judging by the World-Honored One's tone, he seems to praise such a person to the utmost, but in fact he is encouraging us, so that those who hear these words and chapter-and-verse should at once put them into practice; hence his admonition to Subhuti, 'do not speak thus.' For if it were as Subhuti said, later people would certainly think prajna hard to cultivate, and would increasingly push the sage realm far away. In truth it is not hard: one begins precisely at keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. This is the World-Honored One's great compassion and great pity. Subhuti surely knew that to bring forth the mind and cultivate, one must not fall into emptiness; he was only asking on behalf of living beings — which is also great compassion and great pity.

We afflicted living beings, now able to hear these words and chapter-and-verse, are likewise rare, and are likewise those who have planted all good roots at measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas. Were it not so, then this most profound and subtle prajna could not be heard; and even if heard, it would be as if not heard. We are already in a further five hundred years, when strife is firmer still, yet we have been able to come here to read, recite, receive, and uphold. Surely we are those who do not wish to compete, who have few desires and are content, and who are qualified to keep the precepts. If so, we should not belittle ourselves. Those who already keep the precepts should work still harder, and seek to make them firmer. Those who do not should keep them as the Buddha taught, and all Buddhas will greatly rejoice. Let the good roots so planted sprout here. Since we have this qualification, and the World-Honored One's empowerment as well, how can we not exert ourselves?

'Taking these as true': having understood the true meaning, one can also cultivate. Among the six paramitas, whichever one it be, all return to the cultivation of merit. Giving does not necessarily require ruining oneself; one need only relinquish a little wealth according to one's means, so that others benefit — that is the giving of wealth. To speak the Dharma for others, or to give people sutras, is the giving of Dharma, and is no difficult matter. Again, when one urges others to study the Buddha's teaching, one must urge them to keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and seeing those who do not keep the precepts one must urge them all the more. And seeing those who already keep the precepts but do not yet know prajna, one must urge them all the more to understand prajna. The greatness of this merit is inconceivable. Why? Because it perpetuates and exalts the Buddha-seed. One must further urge people to practice the Pure Land quickly and seek rebirth in the West. One should know that prajna and the Pure Land are related most profoundly. It was said above that students of prajna must first not dwell in marks; only by not dwelling in marks can one raise contemplation from the prajna of words, and when contemplation is deep one realizes the prajna of true reality — which is the nature. In practice one begins with contemplation and at the end must realize true reality, and this is not at all easy. In the Saha world, with all its evil enticements, how could one immediately realize true reality? Therefore great bodhisattvas, cultivating and making vows, practice for three asankhyeya kalpas, passing through who knows how many rounds of birth and death. Such a person's good roots are indeed thick; yet even with so long a time as thousands of ten millions of Buddhas and measureless kalpas, he has only been able to give rise to faith. This shows how heavy his karmic obstacles are, and that he must therefore make the vow to seek rebirth in the West. Again, the text above brought forth the great mind: all classes of living beings should be led into remainderless nirvana and delivered. Such deliverance of beings extends upward to the Heaven of Neither Thought Nor No-Thought and downward to the hells. Even if we bring forth this great mind, how can we go and deliver them? This in fact makes us first contemplate the principle that conditioned arising is equal. If one would fulfill the vow, one must first realize the nature; and to realize the nature, one cannot but first seek rebirth in the West. Rebirth in the West is not for one's own sake: it is originally for the sake of delivering living beings, and only thus does it accord with Amitabha's original vow, for by fulfilling the great vow one can realize the nature. Hence the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows says: space is endless, worlds are endless, living beings are endless, my vow is endless. Is this not entirely the same as this sutra's vow to deliver living beings widely? From this one can see that the prajna teaching and the Pure Land teaching are one and not two. Only with this great vow will Amitabha come to receive and guide one, and one's rebirth will not be for one's own sake. Only with the teaching of rebirth can the prajna teaching be accomplished.

Such a person's keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is also extremely difficult; he has already drawn near many Buddhas and planted good roots. From this one can see that to accomplish the prajna teaching one should draw near Amitabha, and only then can the prajna of true reality appear before one. Chan Master Yongming said: one need only see Amitabha — why worry about not opening to awakening? Therefore students of prajna must quickly practice the gate of Buddha-recitation; and those who practice the Pure Land must likewise quickly practice the prajna teaching. If one does not understand this supreme meaning, then one who merely recites the Buddha's name will, I fear, be born only in the lowest grade. Therefore those who promote the Pure Land teaching must not stop at speaking of Buddha-recitation alone. One should know that the practice of the Pure Land is precisely for fulfilling the great vow, and that mere Buddha-recitation resulting in a low-grade birth cannot fulfill it. Chan Master Yongming's verse — 'Without Chan, with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice and ten thousand go; one need only see Amitabha — why worry about not opening to awakening?' — can only be used to encourage the dull, not those of sharp faculties. The world overlooks the phrase 'see Amitabha' and attends only to 'ten thousand practice and ten thousand go,' thinking that one need not practice contemplation according to the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations. This is a mistake. That sutra makes clear the supreme meaning, which is precisely prajna; if one is born only in the lowest grade, one cannot see the Buddha.
(Ren) Second, clarifying his merit. Two parts: (Gui) First, directly clarifying the merit; second, explaining and revealing the reason.
(Gui) First, directly clarifying the merit.

'Hearing such words and chapter-and-verse, even to the point of giving rise to a single moment of pure faith. Subhuti, the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees that these living beings attain such measureless merit.'

'Hearing such words and chapter-and-verse' designates the person who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit. This word 'hearing' answers to the word 'hearing' in the earlier phrase 'hearing such words and chapter-and-verse.' Only when one has heard such words and chapter-and-verse and takes them as true can one give rise to faith. The two words 'pure faith' refer precisely to true faith. What is meant by 'pure'? It is what the later text calls 'when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born.' When such a person works earnestly at contemplation, practicing thus for a long time without the least grasping, pure faith is at once born — and that is true reality. This 'pure' is not spoken in contrast to defilement; it is absolute purity. Since one clings to neither of the two extremes of emptiness and existence, it is true reality. 'Even to the point of' is a word of omission. In giving rise to pure faith there are those whose pure thoughts continue without interruption, and those of many thoughts. At the very least there is the single moment in which pure faith is born, when one can have neither many thoughts nor thought following upon thought without interruption. These two words 'even to' include many people of differing degrees of practice; the later text calls them 'these living beings,' and yet, whatever the depth of their practice, the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees them. 'A single moment' means the arising of a thought, the stirring of the mind. 'Born' is what Nagarjuna meant by 'all dharmas do not arise, yet prajna arises.' From this one can see that without the utmost effort it cannot be born. Moreover, a single moment of response is the root of uninterrupted pure thought, and uninterrupted pure thought comes from a single moment of response. That this single moment is pure, no one can know; only the Tathagata can know and see it, for the pure mind is without marks and cannot be seen by the fleshly eye or the heavenly eye. Yet this explanation is still not the fundamental meaning. One should know that this sentence is precisely a commentary on the arising of pure faith. The Tathagata is the dharma-body; when such a person has a single moment of response, he is mind-to-mind sealed with the Tathagata, and light illumines light. Therefore the Tathagata's 'fully knowing' is knowing within the nature, which is precisely awakening thoroughly to the Buddha-nature; and the Tathagata's 'fully seeing' is the illumination of the nature-light, which is precisely the first opening of the Buddha-eye. This attainment is extraordinary; hence the ancients said: one moment of response, one moment a Buddha — and being a Buddha, how could his merit be measured?

These two small sections are precisely a commentary on 'can give rise to faith' and 'take these as true.' From 'know that such a person' down to 'has already planted all good roots at the places of measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas' explains the cause of keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. From 'hearing such words and chapter-and-verse' down to 'attain such measureless merit' explains the fruit of keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. The World-Honored One praises such a person to the utmost precisely in order to encourage us to bring forth the supreme mind, make great vows, and undertake great practice, and so to attain measureless merit.

Again, from Subhuti's 'do not speak thus' down to 'attain such measureless merit' is precisely a commentary on the earlier section that directly showed, from 'should thus subdue his mind' down to 'then one sees the Tathagata.' The earlier text states the principle; here a concrete person is brought forward to confirm it. One should know that only those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can thus give rise to faith, thus give rise to pure faith, and thus attain measureless merit. The meaning of this sutra's text answers everywhere to itself, its veins running through in just this way.
(Gui) Second, explaining and revealing the reason. Two parts: (Zi) First, direct explanation; second, reverse demonstration.
(Zi) First, direct explanation.
'Why is this? These living beings no longer have the marks of self, person, being, and life span. They have no mark of dharma, and also no mark of no-dharma.'

This is a direct explanation of why faith is born and merit obtained. Why one can give rise to pure faith and why one can attain measureless merit: only by eliminating the discriminating mind can this be done. Once discrimination is eliminated, right faith appears of itself, which is what Nagarjuna meant by 'all dharmas do not arise, only prajna arises.' Though such a person has not yet brought prajna fully before him, he has already given rise to pure faith and is mind-to-mind sealed with the Tathagata, light illumining light, and so attains measureless merit — and this is truly not easy. Because discriminating deluded thoughts are eliminated, he can no longer have the marks of self, person, being, and life span. The phrase 'these living beings' covers a great deal. The earlier 'one who gives rise to pure faith in a single moment' refers to those of the lowest degree; there are still those of many moments of response, with pure thought continuing without interruption, and so it says 'these living beings.' The word 'again' in 'no longer' deserves attention: it says that such a person's self-attachment is already empty and will never recur. The lines 'no mark of dharma' and the rest say that such a person has no dharma-attachment.

The four marks arise from grasping at the mark of self. The sutras give many meanings when speaking of the four marks; here I take those that fit this sutra, which have a narrow and a broad sense. In the narrow sense they refer to grasping at the five aggregates and the physical body. This is the mark of self. Ordinary beings all share this affliction of grasping: they cannot forget anything, not only in the present but also reckoning on the future — after death they may ascend to heaven, or to the heaven of Great Brahma. This is what is called the pudgala, and from it all kinds of deluded thoughts arise, which the Consciousness-Only school calls the universally imagined attachment. Future and present stand in opposition to each other; viewed from the side of that opposition, it is the mark of person. From this body arise growth and decline, suffering and joy, and all the rest, which is the mark of being. Reckoning further that the five aggregates and the physical body continue without the root of life being cut off is the mark of life span. All these are various reckonings and discriminations made upon one's own five aggregates. In the broad sense, one reckons 'I' in all kinds of discrimination. That which stands opposed to it is the person; more than one person is a being; and this reckoning continuing without interruption is the life span. As soon as grasping arises there is a grasper and a grasped: the grasper is the self, the grasped is the person; the various discriminations are the mark of being; and the grasper and grasped continuing without interruption is the mark of life span. One should know that the four marks are opened out from the view of self. Opened, they are four marks; combined, they are the mark of self. Why the World-Honored One opened them out and spoke of them thus has a wondrous meaning. The view of self is discrimination; grasping at self is the seventh consciousness; the arising of discrimination is the sixth consciousness. Prajna is right wisdom; if the prajna of true reality is to appear before one, one must transform the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. When the sixth and seventh are transformed, the fifth and eighth are transformed together; hence the World-Honored One repeatedly spoke of the four marks. When the four marks are empty, self-attachment is empty, which is also called the emptiness of person.

The mark of self is grasping that arises from the body; the mark of dharma is grasping that arises from dharmas. 'No mark of dharma' is the emptiness of dharma-attachment, also called the emptiness of dharmas. 'No dharma' means nothingness, which is emptiness. 'Also no mark of no-dharma' is the emptying of emptiness itself, also called repeated emptiness, also called total emptiness. Prajna reveals the principle of the three emptinesses, and its main work is to dispel grasping. After the person and self are empty, to grasp at the emptiness of dharmas is still impermissible; therefore one must dispel it layer upon layer, until even emptiness must be emptied. The ancients called this 'exhausting emptiness to the very bottom,' which is vastly different from one-sided emptiness; hence it is called ultimate-meaning emptiness, also called supreme-meaning emptiness.

This explains that those in the previous section who have given rise to pure faith can reach the three emptinesses. The three emptinesses contain many principles, measureless in breadth and bottomless in depth — what Samantabhadra's vows call the ocean of most profound teaching. According to the three emptinesses, having no four marks is the emptiness of self; having no mark of dharma is the emptiness of dharmas; and having no mark of no-dharma is the emptiness of emptiness. In fact this is simply the elimination of the two attachments, to self and to dharmas: 'no mark of dharma' empties dharma-attachment, and 'no mark of no-dharma' likewise eliminates dharma-attachment, for no-dharma is fundamentally without dharma. Yet one must not grasp at it either; a single grasping becomes attachment to no-dharma. Therefore the emptying of dharma-attachment by 'no mark of dharma' is the first layer, and the emptying of even the attachment to 'no mark of no-dharma' is the second layer. Taken together, both are dharma-attachment. With the four marks spoken of above, they are set out as the two attachments to self and to dharmas in contrast. That such a person gives rise to pure faith means that the two attachments to self and dharmas are both dispelled. Yet the two attachments to self and dharmas that arise from discrimination are coarse attachment. There are still the innate attachments to self and dharmas, subtle attachments that come from the stirring of thought, called the dormant afflictions, also called the ignorance of the ground of dwelling. Such a person can only eliminate the discriminated attachments to self and dharmas; he cannot eliminate the innate attachments to self and dharmas.

There is another essential meaning. Spoken separately, they are the three emptinesses; spoken together, they are the emptying of the two attachments to self and to dharmas. Yet they may also be viewed from the two extremes of emptiness and existence: the mark of no-dharma is emptiness and belongs to the extreme of emptiness, while self and dharma may be spoken of together and belong to the extreme of existence. That such a person gives rise to pure faith means that he can also not cling to either extreme. The extreme of existence is called the conventional truth, the extreme of emptiness the true truth. Here again the two truths are contained. In other sutras the Buddha speaks of three truths, including the truth of supreme meaning; but prajna, in dispelling grasping, speaks only of the two truths. One should know that negation and illumination occurring at once is precisely the Middle Way; and so in speaking of two truths the three truths are in fact contained. Dispelling the two extremes is double negation, and double negation is double illumination. Yet there must also be negation and illumination at once. Such a person has not yet reached this degree; he can only not cling to the two extremes, as one may see by savoring the text closely. All that the Buddha says is thorough from head to tail and from beginning to end; it must not be read carelessly. Even the above, giving rise to pure faith and attaining measureless merit, has its shallow and its deep aspects. In sum, such a person only eliminates coarse attachment, not subtle attachment. That is why the Buddha speaks ever more deeply, to make clear that such a person's elimination of attachment is still only the first step, and that further effort is needed. Yet such a person has reached no easy point: a single moment of response is already extraordinary. Those who work hard often have this kind of state, feeling the mind hollow and empty, clean and pure; sometimes it lasts half a month or half a year, and all of it is this same scene. One should know that such attainment is still far short, and that one must not be self-satisfied. Otherwise two faults arise: with regard to the sutra's meaning one takes the deep for the shallow, while with regard to oneself one takes the shallow for the deep — not realizing that one is still far, far away! In the case of the person indicated by this sutra, discriminating self-attachment is already eliminated, and though greed, anger, and delusion are not wholly gone they are already very thin; still further effort is required. When we work hard we can measure ourselves and see whether or not we accord with what the sutra says. Speaking of this, I recall an episode from antiquity. When Emperor Suzong and Emperor Daizong of the Tang, father and son, put down the rebellion of An Lushan, Emperor Daizong strove mightily to propagate the Buddha-Dharma, and the Tantric Tripitaka Master Bukong also came to China at that time. Buddhism flourished as never before. One day, when Emperor Daizong was discussing the Buddha-Dharma with the National Master, Yu Chaoyen was beside them and interjected, asking: since the Buddha says all living beings are Buddhas, how does ignorance arise? The National Master at once said: you are not fit to ask this question. Chaoyen was furious, but since the emperor was present he dared not speak, though his anger showed in his face. The National Master then said: ignorance arises from this. Here we can test ourselves. If someone comes to slander and revile me, can I keep from giving rise to anger? If I meet with forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, touches, and dharmas, can I keep from giving rise to thoughts? If I meet with poverty, so that today there is not even rice to eat, can my mind keep from worry? One must act as though nothing were the matter before it will do. Otherwise one clings to the marks of self, person, being, and life span. Yet to be hollow and empty is of course very good; but it is not enough. One should go and practice giving. The six paramitas and the ten thousand practices must all be practiced. If one settles for being hollow and empty, one clings to the mark of no-dharma. If one has a mind to deliver beings, one clings to the mark of dharma. Hence one should know that for such a person to give rise to pure faith and eliminate the discriminating mind is truly not easy. That is why the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees him, and acknowledges that his understanding equals the Buddha's mind, that he has opened the Buddha-eye and attained such measureless merit.

This not only explains the previous section; it also answers back to the whole section that directly showed, for what was not explained above is here pointed out and awakened to. 'All classes of living beings' down to 'I will lead them all into nirvana and deliver them' answers precisely to the mark of dharma. 'In truth no being attains deliverance' answers precisely to the mark of no-dharma. 'If a bodhisattva has the marks of self, person, being, and life span, he is not a bodhisattva' is precisely 'no longer has the marks of self, person, being, and life span.' 'A bodhisattva should practice giving while dwelling nowhere' is relinquishment, which breaks the self; it requires us first to empty the mark of self. 'Not dwelling in marks' is not dwelling in any kind of mark, which is no mark of dharma. Again, the simile of space in the four directions and above and below is no mark of no-dharma. 'If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata' is the fusion of the two extremes. For to see only marks is to cling to existence, and to see only no-marks is to cling to emptiness; but to see marks as no marks is the fusion of the two extremes, which is no mark and yet no absence of marks, and one attains to see true reality — hence it says 'then one sees the Tathagata.' Because one sees the Tathagata, one attains such measureless merit, which is the inconceivable merit spoken of above. The Buddha's meaning is that such a person can understand the Dharma I have spoken above, keep the precepts and cultivate merit, give rise to pure faith, and take these as true, and will of course be without the four marks of self and so on, and attain such measureless merit. This too is to encourage us: if we would cultivate prajna, we should begin thus, and must not fall into emptiness; we should first block up the side of no-dharma, plant our feet on solid ground, and practice in our own persons. To cling to neither the mark of dharma nor the mark of no-dharma is the essential secret of practice.
(Zi) Second, reverse demonstration.

'Why is this? If these living beings' minds grasp at marks, then they cling to self, person, being, and life span. If they grasp at the marks of dharmas, they cling to self, person, being, and life span. Why? If they grasp at the marks of no-dharma, they cling to self, person, being, and life span.'

The previous section is called the direct explanation because it explains from the positive side why faith is pure and why measureless merit is attained: because such a person has already seen the principle of the three emptinesses. To have no marks of self and so on is the emptiness of person (also called the emptiness of self-attachment); to have no mark of dharma is the emptiness of dharmas (also called the emptiness of dharma-attachment); to have no mark of no-dharma is the emptying of emptiness itself (also called total emptiness). These are the three emptinesses. From seeing the three emptinesses, one advances with vigor and one's pure thoughts continue without interruption, and one then realizes the pure dharma-body; hence it says 'attains such measureless merit.'

This section is called the reverse demonstration because it further shows from the negative side why the three emptinesses are indispensable, making clear that the slightest clinging to marks is the discriminating mind and is not the pure nature. Why? Because whatever has marks is false and delusive. Therefore to cling to marks is to pursue the false, and to pursue the false is to lose the true nature. Once the true nature is lost, one is still an ordinary being who gives rise to delusion, creates karma, and receives the suffering retribution of birth and death — how could one attain measureless merit?

From this one can see that the purpose of adding the reverse demonstration after the direct explanation is simply to make living beings quickly awaken: relying on this sutra's principle of non-dwelling, they should on the one hand diligently practice the six paramitas and on the other contemplate no-mark, giving rise to pure faith, in the hope of realizing the nature-essence of the three emptinesses and passing beyond the ordinary into the sage. Such is the general meaning of the necessity of the reverse demonstration.

Yet there is another meaning: it guards against doubts arising in the reader of the preceding text. What doubts? (1) The marks of self and so on arise from the view of the body. The body is the root of suffering, and one should not cling to its marks — this principle is easy to understand. But dharmas are not so: to deliver oneself and others there must be a dharma. Giving and the six paramitas — are there not plainly dharmas here? Having a dharma, there are the marks of that dharma. Now the text says 'no mark of dharma.' If a dharma is without marks, then the dharma too hovers between existence and nonexistence. How then can the mark of dharma be absent? (2) If there is a view of the body, one will inevitably discriminate between self and others; and once there is discrimination, one will inevitably create karma and receive retribution. Therefore one should not have the view of the body, and should not discriminate self and others. But a dharma is not a body — where in it are self and other? Even if one raises discrimination over a dharma, that is to discriminate self and other. As for the two words 'no-dharma,' they are no different from another name for emptiness. Since it is called empty, how can it have marks? Why then does the text put dharma and no-dharma on the same footing as the four marks of self and person that arise from the view of the body, and say that all alike are absent? It is in order to cut off all these doubts that the text must add a clear explanation from the negative side.

'These living beings' refers to the living beings mentioned above who have given rise to pure faith and seen the three emptinesses. The word 'mind' in 'if the mind grasps at marks' is important. One should know that the mind is fundamentally without marks; the word 'marks' need not refer exclusively to the physical body but points rather to all marks of objects. The mind is fundamentally without marks; if there is any kind of mark, then one has grasped at an object. And if one grasps at the marks of objects, has one not already lost one's own mind? This is precisely the appearance of turning from enlightenment and joining with dust, which is why one has become an ordinary being. Hence one should further know: when one grasps at the marks of objects, who is it that grasps? It is not another; it is I. From this one can see that if the mind grasps at marks, it becomes the mark of self. And the marks grasped exist because of the grasping 'I,' just as the mark of person arises from the mark of self; therefore the grasped object becomes the mark of person. The grasped marks pile up and multiply, becoming the mark of being. When those marks continue without interruption, they become the mark of life span. From this it follows that whatever mark one grasps at, there is a grasper and a grasped, multiplying without interruption. Hence it says, 'if the mind grasps at marks, then it clings to self, person, being, and life span.' 'Then it is' means simply 'thereupon is': as soon as one grasps, one has clung. Therefore if one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one likewise clings to the four marks of self, person, being, and life span. How can one say that a dharma is unlike the body, and that there is no self in it? As soon as one grasps there is the discrimination of grasper and grasped; how can one say that discrimination over a dharma is not discrimination of self and other?

From this one can further see that what the previous section calls 'no mark of dharma' means simply not grasping at it; it does not mean that dharmas and marks are ultimately nonexistent. If they were ultimately nonexistent, that would be the mark of annihilation! As for no-dharma, it is of course another name for emptiness, and emptiness is originally without marks. Yet once one grasps at it, there is the grasping 'I' and the grasped 'person,' multiplying without interruption, and the four marks are plainly there. Hence it says, 'if one grasps at the marks of no-dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life span.' I once saw an edition in which someone, I know not who, had deleted the three words 'why is this?' above 'if one grasps at the marks of no-dharma,' thinking that the text ran straight on and its meaning was clear, and that these three words only made the tone tortuous and the meaning unclear. In the Jiaqing period there was an edition which, though it did not dare delete them outright, noted beneath them that the annotations of certain commentators and all the correct texts agreed these were a superfluous line. Those 'certain commentators' were mostly men of the Ming and Qing. From this one can prove that the words and phrases of this sutra differ greatly from the ancient texts; though there are indeed errors of transcription, they have also not escaped arbitrary addition and deletion by the shallow-sighted — truly lamentable. Fortunately, recent editions of the sutra have had this passage restored by clear-eyed men; yet in remote places there are still editions that delete it, and these must on no account be followed.

For the use of these three words contains a subtle meaning and is of critical importance; they must on no account be omitted. Someone says that the three words 'why is this?' are meant to lift up the preceding meaning, so that one knows that if grasping at no-dharma still clings to the four marks, how much more does grasping at dharmas. This meaning is still shallow. For the passage 'if the mind grasps at marks, then it clings to...' has already explained the reason; why need it be lifted up again? What then is the meaning? It guards against those who do not get the point: though they hear that grasping at the marks of dharmas means clinging to the four marks of self, person, being, and life span, they still do not understand what counts as not grasping, their insight is not true, and they may mistakenly grasp at no-dharma while still thinking that they are not grasping at dharmas. Therefore the three words 'why is this?' are used as a warning question, making one think deeply about the reason and not misunderstand. It follows immediately: 'if one grasps at the marks of no-dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life span.' Then one knows that to grasp at no-dharma is still to cling to marks, no different from grasping at dharmas. Does this mean that 'not grasping at dharmas' does not mean ultimately not grasping? If it is not non-grasping, and grasping clings to marks, then one can see that 'not grasping' means causing one not to cling to marks and to return to the nature. What is this meaning? It is to practice the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices widely, while in the mind nothing is going on, still and concentrated, unmoved by anything. This precisely is the true meaning of not grasping at the marks of dharmas. Acting thus, one clings neither to dharmas nor to no-dharma; this is not clinging to the two extremes and according with the Middle Way. Thus with this one sentence 'why is this?' the two lines below about grasping at the marks of no-dharma are nothing other than an annotation on the two lines above about grasping at the marks of dharmas. Such is the wonder of expounding the Dharma. If these three words were deleted, the tone would be flat and parallel, and this meaning could not emerge.

One should know that existence is emptiness, yet existence; emptiness is not an emptiness apart from existence. Hence the Heart Sutra says: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. That is why this sutra everywhere speaks of not grasping, and yet everywhere speaks of not annihilating. Though the words 'not annihilating' are pointed out only at the very end, in fact everything said at the beginning contains the sense that one should not annihilate. For instance, delivering beings without the mark of delivery is by no means only the single line 'in truth no being attains deliverance'; and 'one should practice giving while dwelling nowhere' makes the meaning even clearer. As for 'if one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata,' this is a crystallized saying. 'All marks as no marks' makes clear not grasping; for if one grasps, one sees only marks and does not see the nature. Precisely because one does not grasp, seeing marks is seeing no marks, and one returns to the Tathagata-store nature; hence it says 'one sees the Tathagata.' In sum, marks are originally no fault; the fault lies in grasping. Therefore if one abandons marks and grasps at no-marks, or abandons no-marks and grasps at a nothingness that can negate, the grasping itself becomes a mark and obstructs the self-nature. From this one can know that if only one does not grasp, marks do no harm; but if one does grasp, even no-marks become an obstruction. Why need one annihilate marks in order to see the nature? For this reason he selected keeping the precepts and cultivating merit alone as the faculties capable of faith. For those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit are already not clinging to emptiness, and when prajna perfumes them, once the understanding of wisdom opens they do not grasp at dharmas. Naturally they can neither cling to existence nor again cling to emptiness, and so easily accord with the Middle Way. Compared with those of wild wisdom, the distance is as heaven from earth. Hence the sutras and treatises say: better to cling to existence as to Mount Sumeru than to cling to emptiness as to a mustard seed. This makes clear that for one who clings to existence it is easy to work, while for one who clings to emptiness it is hard to apply a remedy. The word 'grasp' here stands in close contrast to the word 'relinquish' below. Here the text makes clear that one should not grasp at dharmas; it does not say that one may grasp at no-dharma. (This is spoken in terms of the sense.) Below it makes clear that dharmas should be relinquished; it does not say that no-dharma should not be relinquished. The meaning above and below is exactly the same, and both contain the sense that one cannot speak of emptiness apart from existence. In sum, neither extreme should be grasped, which is to say both should be relinquished. Therefore the text below concludes with 'therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at no-dharma,' still pointing back to the Middle Way.

The use of these three words 'why is this?' has yet another meaning. In the previous section, from 'no longer have the marks of self' down to 'also no mark of no-dharma,' the text runs straight on to make clear the three emptinesses, as already explained. In this section, the placing of 'why is this?' between 'if one grasps at dharmas' and 'if one grasps at no-dharma' serves specifically to make clear the principle of not clinging to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, and so to lead into the two lines below beginning 'therefore.' The two lines 'if the mind grasps at marks' and the next are a general statement: 'one should not grasp at marks' is meant to include the marks of the body as well. The marks of the body belong to the extreme of existence, the same as the marks of dharmas, while the marks of no-dharma belong to the extreme of emptiness. If they were not separated here, and the text ran straight on as before, this meaning would not emerge, and the two words 'therefore' below would have nothing to rest on and could not be connected. This shows the excellence of Kumarajiva's translation.
(Ren) Third, concluding and revealing the Middle Way. Two parts: (Gui) First, concluding by double detachment; second, citing the raft simile to reveal the meaning.
(Gui) First, concluding by double detachment.
'Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at no-dharma.'

The word 'therefore' takes up precisely the preceding text. For if one grasps at the marks of dharmas or no-dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life span; hence neither extreme should be grasped. It also answers to the earlier phrase 'no longer' and the rest. For not grasping means no marks, and only with no marks does pure faith arise, so that one is known and seen by the Tathagata and attains measureless merit. In sum, the Buddha's saying this shows precisely the method of practice: first cause one not to grasp at the two extremes, and gradually one can empty marks and purify the mind-ground. Thence faith, understanding, and practice follow, and even at the ultimate one does no more than not cling to the two extremes. For it is by the prajna of contemplation that one realizes the prajna of true reality; and true reality is no mark and yet no absence of marks — is this not not clinging to the two extremes? This is what is called the cause encompassing the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrating the source of the cause.
(Gui) Second, citing the raft simile to reveal the meaning.
'For this reason the Tathagata constantly says: you monks should know that the Dharma I teach is like a raft. The Dharma itself should be relinquished — how much more so no-dharma.'
The 'this' in 'for this reason' takes up precisely the two lines above about not grasping at dharmas, and also echoes from afar the lines from 'no mark of dharma' onward.

The raft simile is a teaching the Tathagata constantly gave. A boat or raft is meant for crossing over; once across, the raft is abandoned. This illustrates that the Buddha-Dharma is for crossing over birth and death: while birth and death are not yet crossed, one cannot be without the Dharma; but once the other shore is reached, the Dharma too is of no use. This shows that the Dharma must not be grasped. It was constantly taught to the disciples in the Agamas.

The line 'the Dharma itself should be relinquished' follows directly from the raft simile. It also refers at once to the earlier 'one should not grasp at dharmas,' and thereby leads into the following 'how much more so no-dharma.' 'How much more so no-dharma' makes clear that no-dharma should be relinquished still more; relinquishing is not grasping. Yet the sense of relinquishing is deeper: it is not merely not grasping. What was previously grasped must now also be relinquished. Ultimately, even the two words 'not grasping' should be relinquished.

The reason for citing the constantly taught raft simile is that on the one hand the present meaning is used to make clear the constant teaching, and on the other the constant teaching is borrowed to make clear the present meaning. That is to say: by the principle that neither dharma nor no-dharma should be grasped, the raft simile that the Tathagata constantly told the monks, though it speaks only of relinquishing the Dharma, must be understood as relinquishing no-dharma along with it. Why? 'The Dharma itself should be relinquished — how much more so no-dharma': that no-dharma should be relinquished still more needs no saying. This shows that there is no small and no great, that all dharmas are equal, and it is to use the present meaning to make clear the constant teaching. Further, to make clear that in the present meaning the two extremes are not grasped — though the words stand in parallel — one should know that no-dharma should all the more not be grasped, so that one does not cling to emptiness. This is to borrow the constant teaching to make clear the present meaning.

The meaning contained in this passage of the sutra is deep and subtle, and is not exhausted by what has been said above. One should know that between the present meaning and the constant teaching there is one point of sharpest conflict, which must be clearly understood. The constant teaching is that when the Dharma is no longer needed, one relinquishes it; but the present teaching, spoken for those who have just brought forth the great mind, is that one should relinquish the Dharma precisely when it is needed.

Because of this sharp conflict, the World-Honored One, guarding against people clinging to the constant teaching and doubting the present meaning, or clinging to the present meaning and doubting the constant teaching, absolutely had to cite it, so that students might thereby see clearly that though the two differ, they are in fact the same.

What is the doubt? The doubt is: if one relinquishes the Dharma precisely when it is needed, then when the Dharma is relinquished, is there not no Dharma? And without Dharma, how shall one deliver? Is this not contrary to the constant teaching? And yet the text also says one should not grasp at no-dharma. Is there, after all, a Dharma or no Dharma? Does one who is not yet delivered need the Dharma or not need the Dharma?

One should know that the meaning spoken here is that neither of the two extremes, existence and nonexistence, may be clung to; this is what is called the supreme meaning of the Middle Way. One should know that not clinging to the two extremes is precisely the double illumination of the two extremes. Not clinging to the two extremes indeed means there is no such thing as a dharma; yet the double illumination of the two extremes also means there is no such thing as no-dharma. Moreover, not clinging is itself double illumination. From this one can know that just when there is no such thing as existence, there is likewise no such thing as nonexistence; and just when there is no such thing as nonexistence, what harm is there in there being no such thing as existence? Think on this, think deeply: is there ultimately a Dharma or no Dharma? Or is existence itself nonexistence, and nonexistence itself existence? Knowing this, one knows that the present meaning and the constant teaching, though they differ, are in fact the same.

Nevertheless, did the Buddha cite the raft simile solely to resolve doubts about the difference between the constant teaching and the present meaning? No. His deep intent was in fact to guard against people clinging to the present meaning and doubting the present meaning. What is that doubt? Have you readers seen it? Consider the two lines 'therefore one should not grasp at dharmas'; though they conclude the preceding text, they are greatly different in depth from what precedes. The World-Honored One, fearing that people would not understand and so generate obstacles, therefore cited the constantly taught raft simile to make it clear. Otherwise, the two lines beginning 'therefore' have already concluded the matter, and there would have been no need to cite the raft simile again. As for all that was said above about not clinging to the two extremes, down to the passage asking whether there is ultimately a Dharma or no Dharma — this is precisely borrowing the constant teaching to make clear the present meaning, lest doubts arise and obstacles be generated over the depth of the present meaning. If so, we should first make clear wherein that depth lies.

Consider the first passage: from 'no longer have the marks of self' down to 'also no mark of no-dharma' — this speaks of no marks. The second passage, from 'if the mind grasps at marks' down to 'if one grasps at no-dharma' and so on, likewise speaks of not grasping at marks. As for the third passage, the two lines beginning 'therefore' say that dharmas and no-dharma alike are not grasped, and not merely that marks are not grasped. Here precisely lies the great difference from the first two passages, and it is precisely here that people are guarded against giving rise to doubt and generating obstacles.

Consider: the first passage speaks of no marks, in order to cut off the doubts that the marks of dharmas cannot be absent and that no-dharma is originally without marks. Therefore the second passage says that grasping means clinging to marks, so that one understands that the 'no' spoken of means causing people not to grasp, and does not mean no dharmas and no marks. Moreover, since grasping means having marks, the marks of no-dharma also should not be grasped. It further points out that not grasping at the marks of dharmas is bounded by not grasping at the marks of no-dharma, so that one may understand that it is not an absolute not grasping at dharmas, but rather that even while one takes up the six paramitas and other dharmas in practice, the mind has no marks of them. Only then will students not lean to one-sided emptiness or one-sided existence, and only then do they have the correct place to begin.

One should know that in the wondrous teaching of prajna, one must be thoroughgoing from the very start. What is thoroughgoing? One must not leave even a shadow of dharma or no-dharma. For since they are named the mark of dharma and the mark of no-dharma, one can know that they are marks of dharma and marks of no-dharma. If one grasps at dharmas or at no-dharma, grasping means having marks — can that still be called not grasping at marks? Therefore what is said before and after is in principle wholly consistent, differing only in the shallowness and depth of the words and their order. Hence the third passage's two lines beginning 'therefore' must be spoken: one should thus thoroughly not grasp, and only that is not grasping at marks. Then, because the mind is pure, one can realize the fruit of the pure dharma-body.

Question: put this way, the Dharma is indeed to be relinquished. And the added line that one should not grasp at no-dharma I also understand: it serves as the boundary for not grasping at dharmas, so that one knows that though one does not grasp at dharmas, one must on no account grasp at no-dharma. But if this is so, then the method of practicing the six paramitas while the mind has no marks of them can no longer apply. Why? Because here the text does not say one should not grasp at the marks of dharmas, but plainly says one should not grasp at dharmas. Where then is one to set to work? Answer: it is precisely for this that the World-Honored One spoke the fourth line, revealing a most wondrous method.

Consider the two important lines in the fourth passage: 'The Dharma itself should be relinquished — how much more so no-dharma.' These two lines are nothing other than an annotation on the two lines beginning 'therefore.' They point directly and tell the student: I am not telling you merely not to grasp at dharmas, but to not grasp at no-dharma together with them. To stop at not grasping at dharmas would turn into having no Dharma, and without Dharma how could one practice and be delivered? If dharmas and no-dharma are both not grasped, this is the wondrous Dharma. Now, the reason the raft simile is cited is that the raft is itself the Dharma. Therefore on the one hand one is made to understand that the constant teaching of relinquishing the Dharma includes relinquishing no-dharma as well, so that one knows that to relinquish both together is the Dharma of the raft simile that the Tathagata constantly taught. Then what is now plainly said to be the not grasping of dharmas and no-dharma together — is this not precisely that Dharma? And on the other hand, one is made to understand that the constantly taught raft simile says that before crossing one cannot be without the Dharma, and once crossed one relinquishes it, so that one knows that since one has not yet crossed, how can one be without the Dharma? Then one will not mistakenly think that 'one should not grasp at dharmas' means having no Dharma. Moreover, since it plainly also says one should not grasp at no-dharma, this is all the more proof that not grasping at dharmas and no-dharma together is precisely the wondrous Dharma revealed to us. Hence the citing of the raft simile is precisely to reveal this.

Question: how is it that not grasping at either together is precisely the wondrous Dharma? This has confused people again — how is it the wondrous Dharma? One should know that in the supreme meaning, dharma and no-dharma are fundamentally unspeakable. There is no such thing as birth and death, no such thing as nirvana, and still less any such thing as deliverance. Even 'not clinging to the two extremes' and 'the double illumination of the two extremes' become superfluous words. One must simply exterminate feeling and intellect and cut off the tangled vines. Just when one is exterminating and cutting off, the path of words is suddenly cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. Then, birth-and-death being extinguished, all space becomes an unmoving place of practice, and throughout space there is a net of pure radiance; and one comes face to face with the Buddhas of the ten directions. At this point, though it is said there is no such thing as deliverance, one has already, leaving no trace, been delivered in just this way. Then one suddenly realizes that even this one phrase 'no such thing as deliverance' is itself a wondrous Dharma that leads people to deliverance. May I ask: this work of exterminating and cutting off — even if one would not call it a Dharma, how can one avoid it? And is not the not grasping of both dharma and no-dharma precisely this exterminating and cutting off? The two sides press in tight, so that as soon as a thought stirs it clings either to this or to that, leaving the discriminating deluded mind no place to stand. It is like suppressing bandits by closing in from both sides, until they have no foothold and naturally submit. This is the method of the sharp knife cutting through tangled hemp; hence it is said: exterminate feeling and intellect, cut off the tangled vines. This is precisely what the bodhisattva Nagarjuna meant by 'all dharmas do not arise, yet prajna arises.' The orthodox essence of prajna is non-dwelling, and not grasping at the two extremes is the ironclad footing of non-dwelling. This itself is the supreme, most profound, wondrous Dharma — what the sutra calls the Dharma of anuttara-bodhi. Because one takes this as the cause of one's fundamental practice, one realizes the fruit of anuttara-bodhi. One should then suddenly understand that it is exactly the same as the raft simile: it is not that there is no Dharma by which to be delivered, and still less that one relinquishes the Dharma before crossing. Yet you doubt how deliverance is to come about, and whether at the time of deliverance there is a Dharma or no Dharma — is this not raving?

Question: why did the Buddha not explain that not grasping is itself the Dharma, but instead let people grasp it for themselves? Answer: this too has a deep purpose. (1) Not grasping is fundamentally not a dharma, and there is no way to name it; it is provisionally called the dharma of no-dharma. Giving, prajna, and the rest are all provisional names; since there is no way to name them, they are tentatively called dharmas — are there really such things? This is so of all worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike. (2) It is precisely because living beings cling everywhere that he speaks of not grasping at the two extremes, in order to cure their disease. If one took this to be the wondrous Dharma, one would again be dwelling and clinging. This is the painstaking care behind his not explaining. Yet the World-Honored One still feared that students, as thoughts stirred, might unawares dwell and cling to this and give rise to discrimination, so that ignorance would still remain and would have to be dispelled further. That is why he also spoke the second round — that is, the latter half of the sutra — precisely for this matter. (3) Though he did not explain, he guarded against people wandering in perplexity with no way to proceed; therefore he cited the raft simile to let slip a little news, so that true cultivators might likewise grasp it for themselves. One should know that in all things, what one grasps for oneself is of use. Why? Because at the very moment one grasps it, one is already receiving its benefit; this is more beneficial than what comes from outside through seeing and hearing. That is why the ancient worthies, in expounding the Dharma, often did not pour it all out — they were guarding against blocking people's gate of awakening.

I have set it all out this time, which is hardly in keeping with the ancient precepts, and I am well aware of the fault. Yet there are also my own small reasons for having to speak. Because the Buddha-Dharma has long declined, most people fear to hear of prajna, and most of those who talk of prajna go astray. And since you are so earnestly seeking the Dharma, if I absolutely did not awaken you a little, I could not open people's true gate of awakening. Moreover, there is something I rely on that makes me unafraid: there is the latter half of the sutra, which very profoundly remedies this disease, so there is no need to fear that hearing it will make one dwell in it. (And by awakening people here first, when we come to the latter half there will already be a groundwork. Here one should urge that no one be absent from a single session, lest what comes before and after fail to connect.)

Speaking to this point, there is one more thing I cannot but offer. Whoever wishes to grasp the true meaning in the sutra has only to read it with utmost sincerity and reverence. Once reading has made it familiar, one should constantly contemplate a passage or two, or a line or two. Contemplation is reflection. Yet this reflection is wholly different in flavor from what is ordinarily called research. Ordinary research into a subject uses ordinary feelings to conjecture; this is not so. Though it does not depart from words either, one must on no account weigh and tap at the words; even if one does, nothing will come of it. One must sweep away all distracting thoughts, quiet the mind and still the thinking, and focus the whole mind upon it. Not weighing and tapping at the words is not grasping at no-dharma; focusing the whole spirit on this sutra is not grasping at dharmas. This is the cultivation of concentration. In time, when not a single thought arises, the light of the nature appears, and the true principle in the sutra naturally wells up. This is reflection-cultivation; only this is receiving and upholding, and only thus can one grasp it. Therefore the moment of grasping is the moment of receiving its benefit. In reading sutras one should read in this way, and then the two studies of concentration and wisdom are cultivated together. One should further repent deeply and seek the empowerment of the Three Jewels. Otherwise, I fear that if one's obstacles are heavy, one will not only fail to grasp it but will not even manage the contemplation well. (Below one must say that not grasping at the two extremes does not mean not practicing giving and the other paramitas.)

Question: if not grasping at the two extremes is the prajna teaching, may one then omit giving and the other dharmas? That is a mistake: to omit giving and the rest is to grasp at no-dharma. One should know that prajna is the mother of giving and the other five paramitas.
