When prajna is born, the five paramitas are born the more along with it, and one practices them all the more wondrously. When one practices the five paramitas with the contemplative wisdom of prajna, then all five are paramitas indeed.

Whenever one sets forth a dharma, there are four alternatives. One may say it exists, or say it does not exist (that is, it is empty), or say it both exists and does not exist, or say it neither exists nor does not exist. In the most profound prajna, all four alternatives are dispelled. This is what is meant by 'free of the four alternatives, cut off from the hundred negations.' (The hundred negations are nothing beyond the four alternatives.) Because the self-nature is pure and unstained by the least dust, all alike should be negated. And these four passages are precisely the freedom from the four alternatives.

The first passage dispels existence by nonexistence. (To cling to existence makes one an ordinary being, so it must be dispelled by nonexistence.) The second passage speaks of both existence and nonexistence, in order to dispel one-sided nonexistence. (Practice, the dharmas of the six paramitas, preserves existence; the mind having no marks of them preserves nonexistence. One-sided nonexistence is guarded against lest one fall into annihilation.) The third passage speaks of neither existence nor nonexistence, in order to dispel both existence and nonexistence. For 'both existence and nonexistence' cannot avoid preserving the two extremes; hence, by saying that neither extreme should be grasped — that is, grasping at existence is wrong and grasping at nonexistence is wrong — the two extremes are no longer kept apart but fused. As for the fourth passage, 'the Dharma itself should be relinquished': the Dharma refers to the six paramitas and the like; 'how much more so no-dharma': no-dharma refers to the dharma of neither existence nor nonexistence. For by the principle that all dharmas do not arise yet prajna arises, the so-called not grasping at the two extremes is carried through to the very end. Therefore, while actually delivering, one begins with both existence and nonexistence and proceeds to neither existence nor nonexistence. Once deliverance is attained, then not only is the dharma of both existence and nonexistence relinquished, but of course the dharma of neither existence nor nonexistence is relinquished together with it; only thus does one become the Tathagata in whom all dharmas are one suchness. This is surely what all Buddhas and Tathagatas constantly taught. Thus our World-Honored One, putting on his robe and eating his food, appeared the same as ordinary beings, and yet his voice and excellent marks were fully present. At this point birth and death and nirvana are both not dwelt in. Does it exist? Does it not exist? Does it both exist and not exist? Does it neither exist nor not exist? All four alternatives are unspeakable.

The two lines 'one should not grasp at dharmas' and 'one should not grasp at no-dharma' are the most essential words. All that was said above is not grasping at the two extremes. Therefore these two lines are nothing other than the concluding words of the preceding text. The passage on the raft simile likewise makes clear that these two lines are the wondrous Dharma, the so-called Dharma of anuttara-bodhi. (This should be explained in detail.)

As said above, what is spoken is the supreme-meaning siddhanta, spoken as an expedient within the unspeakable. All that this sutra says is supreme-meaning siddhanta, and therefore the expounder too cannot but speak thus. Yet when the Buddha's perfect voice is uttered once, no meaning is not encompassed; however one speaks, it is acceptable. What has been said above is very lofty, but there is no harm in explaining it according to the siddhanta of individual adaptation. Individual adaptation means fitting the faculties. The sutra says: this sutra is spoken for those who have brought forth the Mahayana mind, and for those who have brought forth the supreme vehicle's mind. For such faculties it is therefore spoken suddenly and directly. For example: 'no four marks of self and person' is the dharma of the emptiness of self, spoken to deliver from self-attachment. Again: 'no mark of dharma,' 'one should not grasp at dharmas,' 'the Dharma itself should be relinquished' — this is the dharma of the emptiness of dharmas, spoken to deliver from dharma-attachment. Again: 'also no mark of no-dharma,' 'one should not grasp at no-dharma,' 'how much more so no-dharma' — this is the dharma of the emptiness of emptiness, spoken to deliver from the attachment to emptiness. There are very many such teachings; why doubt that without a Dharma one cannot be delivered? One should know that the text says there are no marks of self and person; it does not say there is no self and person. It says there is no mark of dharma and no mark of no-dharma; it does not say that dharmas and no-dharma are ultimately nonexistent. In sum, to say 'no,' to say 'not grasping,' to say 'relinquish,' is only to dispel grasping, not to abandon the dharma itself. Once the three graspings are dispelled, the three emptinesses shine together and the three obstacles are wholly dissolved. Then even birth and death and nirvana are both not dwelt in; how much less could this shore fail to be crossed or the other shore fail to be reached? Let it be explained further according to the siddhanta of counteraction. Counteraction means prescribing the medicine to fit the disease, healing the illness. The sutra says: the disease of living beings lies in clinging everywhere. Therefore the Buddha speaks of emptiness to those who cling to existence, and of existence to those who cling to emptiness, all simply to cure living beings of the disease of one-sided clinging. As soon as there is one-sided clinging, one does not accord with the nature-essence; one turns from enlightenment and joins with dust, so that karmic obstacles multiply and suffering is endless. Hence counteraction is needed. Thus here the text says the Dharma should be relinquished, and then says no-dharma should be relinquished still more. (Relinquishing is not grasping, which is also no marks; this is spoken in terms of the sense, not strictly according to the words.) From this one knows that 'relinquishing the Dharma' means relinquishing the disease of clinging to existence. Again, since it says both that no-dharma should be relinquished and that the Dharma should be relinquished, one knows that 'relinquishing no-dharma' means relinquishing the disease of clinging to emptiness. When the disease is gone, existence becomes wondrous existence and emptiness is true emptiness. One should know that to speak of wondrous existence makes clear that it exists yet does not exist, and therefore wondrous existence is true emptiness. To speak of true emptiness makes clear that it is empty yet not empty, and therefore true emptiness is wondrous existence. From this one can see that the reason one is made from the very start not to grasp at the two extremes is precisely so that one may attain the double illumination of the two extremes. Double illumination is alert yet still, still yet alert — what is called stillness and illumination at once. 'At once' means still and yet constantly illuminating, illuminating and yet constantly still; this is the samadhi of still illumination and suchness, this is the Buddha's realm. At this stage one not only extinguishes the obstacle of afflictions but extinguishes the obstacle of the known as well; one not only crosses fragmentary birth and death but crosses transformation birth and death too. This is what is meant by 'lead them all into remainderless nirvana and deliver them.' From this one can see that all said here is the utterly perfect and utterly sudden supreme wondrous Dharma that directly causes one to become a Buddha. Whatever practice one undertakes, if one can grasp the meaning here and act accordingly, one's attainment will surely be swift and high. Moreover, the method is direct and to the point; if one calls it difficult, it is in fact not difficult. All you good friends, the Buddha-Dharma is hard to hear and yet you have heard it; the Buddha's kindness is hard to repay and yet it must be repaid — it lies only in our taking it up directly.

blocks.text: Nothing Attained, Nothing Spoken, Part Seven

inline.s: (Ren) Fourth, question, explanation, and confirmation. Three parts: (Gui) First, asking by citing the Tathagata's fruition-virtue; second, explaining by the ungraspability of dharmas; third, confirming by citing the unconditioned of all.
(Gui) First, asking by citing the Tathagata's fruition-virtue.
'Subhuti, what do you think? Has the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Has the Tathagata spoken any Dharma?'

This passage on question, explanation, and confirmation is again an explanation of the reason for the two lines 'one should not grasp' — how it is that one does not grasp at the two extremes, and why one must not grasp at the two extremes — and it cites the ground of fruition to confirm the ground of practice, to make clear that cause and fruition must be consistent. Therefore the World-Honored One cited the ultimate fruition and asked Subhuti, and after the explanation he further cited all worthies and sages in confirmation. All worthies and sages, viewed from the ultimate fruition, are the cause; but viewed from the beginner who has just brought forth the mind, they are the fruition. (This is divided into three small passages.) The sentences of the sutra often say one thing while meaning another, their gaze darting in all directions and wholly adaptable. Thus in the question here, looking at the two interrogative particles, the words plainly contain 'nothing attained, nothing spoken.' Yet if one said nothing is attained or spoken, one would be grasping at no-dharma; and if one said something is attained or spoken, one would be grasping at dharmas. The raising of this question is therefore a test of whether the hearer of the Dharma can truly comprehend the true meaning of not grasping at the two extremes.

Wherever this sutra places the four words 'what do you think,' in a shallow sense it is a test of whether the hearer of the Dharma can understand what has been said above. In a deep sense it points out to us who read and recite that we must not misconstrue the Buddha's intent, and that we must deeply experience the words that follow; only that is right knowledge and right view, and otherwise we do not accord with the Buddha's intent. In his question the Buddha says 'Tathagata,' yet in Subhuti's answer there appear all worthies and sages; from this one can see that whether one becomes a worthy, a sage, or a Tathagata, one cannot do so without this teaching. The two lines about the Tathagata follow closely upon the two lines about not grasping at dharmas. At first glance the word 'attained' seems to imply attainment, and 'spoken some Dharma' seems to imply speaking. The Buddha's meaning is plainly to ask whether the Tathagata, with regard to the Dharma he spoke, has anything spoken in his mind. That Dharma refers precisely to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Why did the Tathagata speak the Dharma? Precisely so that all living beings might realize supreme bodhi and thereby become Tathagatas — so of course there is attainment. The two interrogative particles in the question are on the surface about dharmas, but inwardly they contain no-dharma as well; for he feared that the careless might misunderstand, and he wanted Subhuti to explain. This not only tests whether the hearers can understand the principle of not clinging to the two extremes, but also points out to us that in our practice we cannot but begin from not clinging to the two extremes.

The careless person at once doubts: did not the Buddha attain the fruition by becoming enlightened beneath the bodhi tree? And were not the forty-nine years of teaching Dharma? How then can we who have just brought forth the mind be told not to grasp at dharmas? Once Subhuti explains — 'the World-Honored One attained yet without attaining, spoke yet without speaking' — the doubt is resolved. Going a step further: the text does not say the World-Honored One attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, nor does it say 'Buddha,' but says 'Tathagata.' The Tathagata is the dharma-body, the virtue of the nature. The Buddha-nature is possessed by everyone; it is only that ordinary beings hide it within the shell of ignorance. Hence these two lines are spoken to make us realize the nature. In the nature, is there anything attained? Is there anything spoken?
(Gui) Second, explaining by the ungraspability of dharmas. Two parts: (Zi) First, clarifying that there is no fixed dharma; second, explaining the double negation.
(Zi) First, clarifying that there is no fixed dharma.
Subhuti said: 'As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; and there is no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can speak.'

This answer is utterly perfect and utterly wondrous. It seems that what is answered is not what was asked. The World-Honored One asked from the side of the one who attains and the one who speaks, while the Elder answered from the side of what is attained and what is spoken. The question is one side, the answer another, and this is most perfect and wondrous. His meaning is: you, venerable sir, ask whether the Tathagata has anything attained or spoken. I have not yet become a Buddha — how should I know? So I merely take the side of the Dharma that is spoken, and briefly explain it according to the meaning the Buddha has always taught. In this way he keeps his proper place: since I have not realized Buddhahood, of course I cannot know; but if I comprehend according to the principle the World-Honored One has taught, I should not go wrong. In saying this the Elder on the one hand considers his own position and on the other reveals it to us. The World-Honored One's speaking of these two lines is of the utmost importance, and we should follow the Elder's intent and go on to comprehend it.

In the Elder's answer he does not say 'Tathagata' but says 'Buddha,' which has a deep meaning. His meaning is that good men and good women who wish to realize supreme bodhi should act according to the Buddha who has already realized the fruition. 'There is no fixed dharma' means that dharmas have no fixity. Put simply, it means that dharmas cannot be clung to; and 'there is no fixed dharma' is thus a commentary on the ungraspability of dharmas.

Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi has not even a fixed dharma by which it can be named; thus the meaning of the answer to the earlier question about attainment and speaking is already clear. If dharmas have not even a fixed name, how much less is there attainment? And how much less still anything spoken? Why did the Buddha, to good men and good women who have brought forth the bodhi mind, not speak of supreme bodhi but say that they should practice giving? From this one can see that apart from all dharmas there is no anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; hence there is no fixed dharma. The speaking of dharmas is always expedient; hence there is also no fixed dharma that can be spoken.
(Zi) Second, explaining the double negation.
'Why is this? The Dharma spoken by the Tathagata is wholly ungraspable and unspeakable, neither dharma nor no-dharma.'

The double negation is 'neither dharma nor no-dharma,' which is double detachment, which is also double negation, meaning that both are negated. These few words of the Elder are utterly perfect and wondrous and admit of all kinds of explanation. The sentences of the sutras should be viewed from every side; the Buddha himself said that in expounding the Dharma through endless kalpas he could not exhaust it — how much more should we ordinary beings comprehend it from many sides? 'No fixed dharma, and no fixed dharma that can be spoken' is understood from the preceding anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. The Elder is saying: how is it that I understand there is no fixed dharma and no fixed dharma that can be spoken? Because the Dharma spoken by the Tathagata is supreme enlightenment, is ultimate enlightenment. Ultimate enlightenment is no-thought. Why? The sutra says that by detaching from subtle thoughts one illumines the mind-nature, and this is called ultimate enlightenment; from this one can see that ultimate enlightenment is no-thought. How can no-thought be grasped? Only when the mind stirs can there be grasping. Both the grasper and the grasped must be done away with, hence it says 'wholly ungraspable.' The World-Honored One, wishing to point out our practice, therefore struck at it from the side and spoke with effort. And the prajna mind-nature is free of the mark of speech, with nothing whatever that speaks or is spoken; hence it says 'wholly unspeakable.' If we cling to the idea that there really is an anuttara-samyak-sambodhi to be realized, we are wrong; hence it says 'neither dharma.' But if we cling to the idea that there is no anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, that too is wrong; hence it says 'nor no-dharma.'

Again, the word 'dharma' in 'the Dharma spoken by the Tathagata' refers to all dharmas. For all dharmas are anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. The Dharma spoken by the Tathagata tells us not to grasp. Yet he plainly also speaks of many dharmas and tells us not to grasp at no-dharma. Therefore we who hear the Dharma should grasp neither dharmas nor no-dharma. From this one knows that the one who speaks the Dharma also speaks only because he cannot do otherwise, and speaks according to the faculties. Since dharmas have no fixity, it is clear that to grasp at dharmas is wrong. But since he plainly speaks dharmas, it is clear that to grasp at no-dharma is wrong too. The two phrases 'neither dharma' and 'nor no-dharma' are precisely a commentary on 'one should not grasp at dharmas' and 'one should not grasp at no-dharma.' Why should one not grasp at dharmas? Because they are neither dharmas. Why should one not grasp at no-dharma? Because they are nor no-dharma. 'Neither dharma nor no-dharma' may also be viewed in reverse: the Tathagata's speaking of neither dharma nor no-dharma is wholly ungraspable and unspeakable.

The Elder says that there is also no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can speak. He specifically brings up the two words 'Tathagata' because the Tathagata is the dharma-body. The dharma-body is without marks — how could there be anything spoken? It contains the sense that the manifestation body, having marks, can speak; hence it says 'no fixed dharma.' 'No fixed dharma' means that one can neither insist that there is a dharma that can be spoken nor insist that there is no dharma that can be spoken. The dharma-body is the nature, and the nature is the great ocean of perfect enlightenment, measureless and boundless. All living beings and all bodhisattvas, viewed from the nature, are one true dharma-realm. Therefore the World-Honored One's speaking of the Dharma flows freely out of the great ocean of perfect enlightenment. If we would realize the great ocean of perfect enlightenment, we should first detach from the mark of mental conditions — how then can there be grasping? And we should detach from the mark of speech — how then can there be speaking? To detach from the mark of speech is precisely for the path of words to be cut off; to detach from the mark of mental conditions is precisely for the sphere of mental activity to be extinguished. Since the sphere of mental activity is extinguished and the path of words is cut off, how can there be discrimination? Hence it says 'neither dharma nor no-dharma.'

It was said above that no-thought means precisely detaching from the discriminating mind. Hence it says one should not grasp at dharmas and should not grasp at no-dharma. The World-Honored One realized the dharma-body Tathagata. Though there is attainment, there is nothing attained; though there is speaking, there is nothing spoken. To attain double illumination, one must first attain double detachment. The two things the World-Honored One asked contain this meaning. Would one say the dharma-body still has something attained? Would one say the dharma-body still has something spoken? The reason the Tathagata is called the Tathagata is that he first detached from discrimination. You who cultivate on the ground of practice should likewise first detach from discrimination; how can you hold the view that there is something attained or something spoken?
(Gui) Third, confirming by citing the unconditioned of all.
'Why is this? All worthies and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma.'

'Why is this?' points out the reason why both extremes must be negated. All worthies and sages use this method of double negation; how can we ordinary beings not use it? The ten dwellings, ten practices, ten dedications, and the four preliminary practices are the worthies; from the first ground to equal enlightenment are the sages; the Tathagata is the utmost sage. Hence it says 'all.' The unconditioned is nirvana. Nirvana in full Sanskrit is parinirvana, translated as quiescent extinction, or as neither arising nor perishing; Kumarajiva, following the old Chinese term, translated it as 'unconditioned.' The Tang Tripitaka Master Xuanzang did not approve of using the old term, because the old term and the original Sanskrit meaning are not entirely the same; hence all the terms he translated were newly coined, to prevent readers from misunderstanding. The unconditioned here means neither arising nor perishing, and is different from Laozi's unconditioned, which is purely following nature without contrivance. To use the new translation is of course appropriate. But Xuanzang also coined many new terms where misunderstanding would not arise, and we do not approve of that either.

The unconditioned refers to the pure mind of the self-nature, which is complete from the first and has no mark of contrivance. When the sutras say there is no cultivation and no realization, they refer to this. One need only extinguish the mind of birth and death, and this quiescent extinction appears before one. As for the method of practice, it is the above 'neither dharma nor no-dharma,' not grasping at the two extremes. One must not grasp at the two extremes and must wholly eliminate discriminating deluded thoughts before it will do. Therefore in becoming a worthy or a sage, all use this method. Worthies and sages differ greatly: viewed with respect to the Tathagata they are the ground of practice, while viewed with respect to ordinary beings they are the fruition. Moreover, each later one viewed with respect to the earlier ones is a fruition, and each earlier one viewed with respect to the later ones is a cause. Hence it says 'all.' Worthies and sages realize the fruit by this unconditioned, hence it says 'all by.' So too with the Tathagata. Whatever the Tathagata speaks, he relies on the unconditioned that he has himself realized, so it cannot be called 'neither dharma.' Yet worthies and sages differ, their positions shallow or deep; from this one knows that whatever the Tathagata speaks accords with the faculties and is expedient, not ultimate truth, so it cannot be called 'nor no-dharma.'

Whatever the World-Honored One spoke, there is no shallow that is not deep and no deep that is not shallow. Therefore he taught the beginner to work from 'one should not grasp at dharmas' and 'one should not grasp at no-dharma.' When the fruit is ripened, even at the deepest stage of practice, it is still this method. We should begin at the stirring of thought, first contemplating no-thought. If one can know it the moment a thought stirs and immediately look back, one can illuminate and abide, and the thought is then no more; yet this is impossible without long practice. Hence at the first stage one must observe, and observation cannot do without deep reflection. In deep reflection one observes: these many thoughts, where do they arise from? As soon as one observes, one sees that arising is no arising, that they are fundamentally false and deluded; and when they arise again, one observes again. Working thus repeatedly, one can illuminate and abide, and can be without thought. Master Datian judged this section to be about the arising of faith, which is deeply apt. For the sutra text says 'can give rise to faith and take these as true,' and 'a single moment gives rise to pure faith' — plainly speaking of faith. The Tathagata became the Tathagata by this method, and all worthies and sages were accomplished by this method; therefore we cannot but thus give rise to faith and take these as true.

blocks.text: According to the Dharma Is Born, Part Eight

inline.s: (Xin) Third, comparing superiority. Four parts: (Ren) First, the merit of giving is great. Two parts: (Gui) First, raising the matter and asking; second, answering and explaining the reason.
(Gui) First, raising the matter and asking.
'Subhuti, what do you think? If a person filled the three-thousand great thousandfold world with the seven treasures and gave them away in giving, would the merit he obtains be great?'

'Comparing' means comparing and measuring; 'superiority' means surpassing excellence. That is, with regard to merit, wisdom is used to compare and measure. Someone says: this sutra teaches people not to dwell in marks, so why does it everywhere compare and measure by merit? This has four essential meanings:

First, it makes one understand that merit and wisdom should both be cultivated. To cultivate wisdom alone without merit will not do. Suppose one expounds the sutras and speaks the Dharma; this is originally to deliver living beings. But living beings happen not to like hearing what you say — this is because you lack merit. Therefore merit is very important. To cultivate both merit and wisdom is to make one complete in compassion and wisdom: wisdom is the wisdom, compassion is the merit. All Buddhas and Tathagatas take the mind of great compassion as their essence. Because great compassion arises toward living beings, the Mahayana Buddha-Dharma is established on the side of living beings. Reading the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows, one knows that Samantabhadra's vow was brought forth from great compassion. In one passage it says: 'Or again, if a person with deep faith receives, upholds, reads, and recites these great vows, or even writes out one four-line verse, he can quickly extinguish the five uninterrupted karmic offenses.' It also says he quickly accomplishes a wondrous form-body complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man. From this one knows that if living beings can fulfill Samantabhadra's merit, they can extinguish offenses and obtain merit. And to practice Samantabhadra's vows, one must first bring forth the mind of great compassion. Therefore compassion is merit. The merit spoken of in this sutra all arises from great compassion; it does not make people seek the blessed rewards of gods and humans.

Second, since merit is so important, one should bring forth the mind of great compassion. Yet without wisdom the bodhisattva path cannot be practiced; hence great wisdom is even more important. The ancients spoke of the two wheels of merit and wisdom. From this one can see that the Tathagata must have both wheels before he can carry on his teaching. Yet the strength of the two wheels is like the left and right hands, with the right side weighted more heavily. Merit is indeed essential, but wisdom is even more so. Therefore filling the three-thousand great thousandfold world with the seven treasures and giving them away is not equal to receiving and upholding a four-line verse and speaking it for others.

Third, by means of this comparison of superiority the preceding text is drawn together. Though the Buddha's speaking of the Dharma is a continuous discourse, in the midst of it he always draws things together at each point. The places in this sutra where superiority is compared are the places where the words and chapter-and-verse are drawn together.

Fourth, this sutra compares superiority many times, and each time the superiority is increased, so that the more it compares the more superior it becomes. This is not because the later text is deeper than the earlier and the difference so great; it is spoken with respect to living beings, indicating that the more excellent one's practice, the more merit one obtains.

The word 'if' is a word of hypothesis; there need not really be such a matter or such a person. In the sutras, the giving that fills the three-thousand great thousandfold world with the seven treasures is what the Great Brahma Heaven King did in a former life, during the time of his causal practice. It was not in one life but through many lives of giving, accumulated until there was this much. The Buddha says 'if there were such a person,' from which one can know that at that time there was no such person.

The sutras say that the greatest mountain in the world is called Mount Sumeru, also called Sumeru-lou, translated as Wondrous Height. This mountain enters the sea for eighty thousand yojanas and rises above the sea for eighty thousand yojanas (one yojana is forty li in Chinese measure), and so is extremely high. It is not made of earth and stone but of the four treasures of gold, silver, vaidurya, and crystal; hence it is called wondrous. Surrounding this mountain is a great sea called the Fragrant Water Sea. Around it again there are seas and mountains, seven layers in all, called the seven fragrant seas and the seven golden mountains. Beyond these there is another great sea called the Salt Water Sea. Around its edge is a great mountain called the Great Iron Enclosing Mountain. Beyond that mountain there are four great continents. One of the four is the southern continent of Jambudvipa, where we dwell. That the world takes the four continents of the globe to be the four continents of the sutras is a mistake. These four great continents, also called the four-under-heaven, lie on the slopes of Mount Sumeru. Of the six heavens of desire, the one nearest the human realm is the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, whose palace lies on the slope of Mount Sumeru. The Four Heavenly Kings govern the human realm and the ghost realm; to inspect the good and evil of the human world is their duty. Above them is the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, which is likewise not in empty space but on the summit of Mount Sumeru. The Jade Emperor of Daoism and the August Sovereign on High of Confucianism are this heaven; from the Four Heavenly Kings down through the six paths, all are under the rule of this heaven. Four heavens further up are in empty space. Above the desire realm, the form realm has eighteen heavens, divided among the first, second, third, and fourth dhyanas. To be born in these heavens requires not only merit but also the power of concentration. There is no longer sexual desire, yet there is still material substance; hence it is called the form realm. To attain birth in the first dhyana one need not practice the concentration of the Buddhist gate; even the concentration of non-Buddhists can bring one to this heaven, as with the Great Luotian Heaven of Daoism. That too is the first dhyana, and Buddhists who practice concentration without escaping the three realms are also lodged in this heaven; hence they are all called dhyana. The Great Brahma Heaven King of the first dhyana has authority above Shakra Devanam Indra. Shakra governs one four-under-heaven, while the Great Brahma King governs a three-thousand great thousandfold world. The Saha world taught by Shakyamuni is as great as this. The world governed by each Buddha is likewise so, differing only as pure or defiled. Even the Land of Ultimate Bliss is this great; but its land is level and made of the seven treasures, in stark contrast to the unevenness here produced by the perilous and evil minds of beings. When living beings cultivate great merit, they are rewarded with an abundance of the seven treasures; when their merit is small, the seven treasures are hidden. These gold, silver, vaidurya, crystal, mother-of-pearl, red pearl, and carnelian are all things not made by present-day human craft. That this person gave away the seven treasures filling a three-thousand great thousandfold world to living beings is likewise beyond human power. 'Would it be' means 'could it be called.' The World-Honored One's question is extremely skillful. It tests not only Subhuti but us as well; for he feared that we might misunderstand the preceding teaching of not dwelling in marks, thinking that since one does not dwell in marks, what need is there of merit? One should know that this person's giving that fills a three-thousand great thousandfold world is itself the delivering of living beings. Therefore one may only not dwell in marks; one must not fail to practice giving. Otherwise it is not the mind of great compassion.
(Gui) Second, answering and explaining the reason.
Subhuti said: 'Very great, World-Honored One. Why? This merit is precisely not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathagata speaks of much merit.'

This answer is deep and meaningful. Subhuti understood the World-Honored One's intent, and so said 'very great.' Yet he also feared that people would not understand: earlier the text plainly said not to dwell in marks, and now it suddenly says 'very great' — is not this petty calculation and measuring a dwelling in marks? Under 'why is this?' he himself explains the reason for answering 'very great.' In this sutra there are many sentences of the form 'is named, precisely is not.' This is the first place where they appear, and so the meaning is stated in fuller detail. He specifically brings out the word 'nature,' so that people may understand that wherever 'precisely is not' is said hereafter, it refers to the nature. 'Therefore it is said' means 'is named,' so that people may understand that wherever 'is named' is said hereafter, it refers to marks. With regard to marks: a name is the mark of a name, and speech is the mark of speech. Whatever is great or small, long or short, high or low, far or near, inner or outer — all that stands in opposition is a mark. Marks change and move, and are false and deluded; the nature does not move, and is empty and still. Therefore with regard to the nature, nothing can be spoken. Subhuti's meaning is: if the marks of merit can be spoken of as much, then it is not the nature of merit; but if it is the nature of merit, empty and still, then even the two words 'merit and virtue' cannot be affixed to it, and how much could be said about its quantity? Wherever 'precisely is not' and 'is named' appear hereafter, they should be understood in this way. Here the two words 'the Tathagata' are specifically added, for the Tathagata is a name for the nature-essence. To say that merit is much is spoken with regard to marks. Why bring up the Tathagata? This contains an essential meaning. The nature is the inner, marks the outer; the nature is the root, marks the branches. Only when there is an inner is there an outer, and only when there is a root are there branches. The meaning is that only with the Tathagata's nature is there merit to speak of; if there were no nature, what merit could be spoken of? 'This merit is precisely not the nature of merit' says 'merit' on the surface but in fact points out that we must not cling to marks. 'Therefore the Tathagata speaks of much merit' means that only with this nature are there these marks, causing us to return from marks to the nature.
(Ren) Second, the superiority of faith in this sutra.
'If again there is a person who, within this sutra, receives and upholds even so little as a four-line verse, and speaks it for others, his merit surpasses that.'

This section is the Buddha's word, and should have 'the Buddha said' or 'Subhuti' before it, which is here omitted. The word 'again' in 'if again' means 'further.' Readers may misunderstand, thinking that to read and recite the Diamond Sutra brings merit surpassing that of the Great Brahma Heaven King. In fact one should attend to the two words 'receive and uphold.' Only if such a person can receive and uphold this sutra and can also give does he surpass that one. 'Receive' is to take in and accept; it means one who can truly comprehend the meaning of the sutra and receive its benefit, one step beyond 'understand.' 'Uphold' means to hold it fast to the breast and never for a moment let it go, one step beyond 'receive.' Since one who receives and upholds it will certainly read and recite it, only the two words 'receive and uphold' are used. 'Even so little as' is a word of omission: whether one receives and upholds the whole or a part, at the least four lines, and so the word 'and so on' is placed. The character 'ge' in 'verse' was originally pronounced 'jie,' and the ancient worthies changed it to the departing tone, just as with the character 'jie' in 'understand.' This is originally Indian poetry; because rhymed text is hard to translate, when it was translated it was sometimes rhymed and sometimes not, and so it was specially renamed 'verse recitation.' In the Indian original, every four lines make a stanza. This 'four-line verse' does not designate any particular four lines in the sutra; any four lines may be so called. The above is self-benefit. The following 'speaks it for others' is benefiting others. The word 'his' refers to the merit of upholding and speaking. 'Surpasses that' means it exceeds the former person's, for he only accomplished giving, and that the giving of wealth, which is the mark of merit. Such a person can both receive and uphold in order to cultivate wisdom, and practice the giving of Dharma in order to cultivate merit. Cultivating both merit and wisdom and being complete in compassion and wisdom is the nature of merit; therefore he surpasses that one.
(Ren) Third, explaining and accomplishing the sutra's power.
'Why is this? Subhuti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.'
